title: Heart route rescue
subtitle: A two-loop delivery system with one muscular pump
objective: Trace blood through the heart, lungs and body and explain the heart’s pumping job.

sow.exactOutcome: Describe the human circulatory system and the job of the heart.
sow.alignment: Directly develops this stated outcome with secondary-age tasks at an upper-KS2 conceptual level. Support and stretch are flexible; this exemplar is not a claim of qualification approval.

success: Explain that arteries carry blood away and veins return it.
Correct a reversed arrow or oxygen-colour misconception.

vocabulary.meaning: A muscular organ that pumps blood.
A blood vessel carrying blood away from the heart.
A blood vessel carrying blood towards the heart.
A very small vessel where substances pass between blood and tissues.
Containing more oxygen than the returning oxygen-poor blood.
A structure that helps prevent backward flow.

equipment: Shared route sheet, pencils, optional tokens moved on the desk.
preparation: Explain that right/left refer to the person’s heart; the route map is not an anatomical front view.
safety: Use desk tokens; no pulse measurements, exercise, bodily samples or physical restraint.
Do not infer a pupil’s health from participation or prior knowledge.
practicalAlternative: Desk route rescue uses supplied labels and arrows; no practical physiological measurements.

misconceptions.correction: Human blood is red; blue in this model means oxygen-poor.
misconceptions.check: Ask what the blue line stands for.

misconceptions.correction: Arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart; the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood.
misconceptions.check: Ask the direction of blood in the heart-to-lungs route.

misconceptions.correction: In a complete circuit it passes through the heart between the lungs and body.

access.supported: Use numbered route words and direction choices.
access.standard: Trace both loops and justify artery/vein names.
access.stretch: Repair a faulty full route and evaluate model limitations.
access.regulation: Offer quiet pointing, private writing, drawing or adult scribing. Pass-and-return for public questions. Use fictional cases; no personal medical disclosure or comparison of bodies. Assign response routes from current evidence, not fixed pupil labels.

slides.title: The courier has lost the route
body: A blood token must visit lungs and body.
Can you rescue its route without skipping the heart?
slides.notes: Pupils trace an imagined token at a desk. The model represents blood flow, not a blood cell choosing where to go.

slides.title: Which system does the delivery?
body: R1. What does the heart pump?
R2. What do blood vessels carry?
R3. Name a substance tissues need.
slides.notes: R1/R2 blood. R3 oxygen, nutrients or water. Establish that lungs supply oxygen to blood, not the heart.

slides.title: I trace one complete journey
body: Start at the right side of the heart.
Visit lungs, then the left heart, then body.
The heart is passed twice per complete circuit.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I follow arrows, not colour alone. Right heart sends blood to lungs. Blood gains oxygen there; returns to left heart; is pumped to body. From tissues it returns to right heart. This is a route map, not anatomical position. Oxygen-poor still contains some oxygen.

visual.title: One complete route: two heart sides
visual.description:
Clockwise sequence: Right heart
pumps to lungs; Lungs
oxygen enters blood; Left heart
pumps to body; Body tissues
use oxygen. Clockwise. Colour marks oxygen content,
not the actual colour of blood.

elements.text: One complete route: two heart sides

Clockwise. Colour marks oxygen content,
not the actual colour of blood.

slides.title: I name the vessel by direction
body: An artery carries blood away from the heart.
A vein carries blood towards the heart.
Oxygen content does not define the name.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Think aloud: Heart-to-lungs is away, so it is an artery even though oxygen-poor. Lungs-to-heart is towards, so a vein even though oxygen-rich. The visual shows one outward route and names the return.

visual.title: Name vessels by their direction
visual.description:
A simplified scientific sequence: Heart; Artery:
away from heart; Body tissues. The return route uses veins towards the heart.
The heart-to-lungs artery also goes away.

elements.text:
The return route uses veins towards the heart.
The heart-to-lungs artery also goes away.

slides.title: I explain the pump
body: Heart muscle contracts to move blood.
Valves help stop backward flow.
A valve guides flow; it does not power the pump.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Trace forward flow through open valve. On the second panel show attempted reverse direction meeting closed leaflets. This is a schematic teaching model, not a surgical drawing.

visual.title: A pumping chamber and a one-way valve
visual.description: Schematic cross-section: muscular wall squeezes the chamber, forcing blood through an open outlet valve. A second panel shows a closed valve resisting reverse flow.

elements.text: Muscle pumps; valves guide the flow
Selective model: chamber shape and scale simplified.

slides.title: Route rescue: four delivery links
body: Use the route clues on page 1.
W1. Put A–D into a complete cycle.
Start with A. Explain the next step.
slides.notes: A right heart→lungs; B lungs→left heart; C left heart→body; D body→right heart. Desk cards or spoken sequence. Ask pupils to identify where oxygen enters and where it is used.

slides.title: Find the two broken labels
body: Fault 1: “Lungs → body, skipping the heart.”
Fault 2: “All veins contain blue blood.”
W2. Repair each with a scientific reason.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Fault1 requires lungs→left heart→body. Fault2 blood is red; veins lead towards heart and can carry oxygen-rich blood, e.g. pulmonary veins. Use two separate reasons.

slides.title: An oxygen-poor artery?
body: W3. The vessel goes from heart to lungs.
Is it an artery or vein?
Decide using direction, then explain colour.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. It is the pulmonary artery, carrying oxygen-poor blood away. Blue is only a key. Do not require pulmonary for supported route.
slides.reveal: Artery: it goes away from the heart. Blue means oxygen-poor in this model.

slides.title: Blood leaves the lungs. Where next?
body: Choose the next main destination in this route.
slides.notes: A is incorrect: blood passes through the left heart before the body. B is correct. C is incorrect: the right heart sends blood to the lungs. Re-trace the lung route if responses are split.

options.text: Straight to the body, bypassing the heart.
options.feedback: Blood returns to the left heart before being pumped to the body.

options.text: To the left side of the heart.
options.feedback: The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

options.text: To the right side of the heart.
options.feedback: The right side receives blood returning from the body.

slides.title: Build a reliable route map
body: Choose one response route.
Show the arrows and explain the pump.
Use the evidence sheet if needed.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across You do. All routes assess circulation, direction and pumping. Differentiate recording, not the core idea.

slides.title: Read your route aloud or silently
body: Can a token follow every arrow?
Does it return to where it started?
Have you passed through both heart sides?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Adult may point to a gap without providing the destination. Tokens need not physically move around the room.

slides.title: Check the key
body: Write “oxygen-rich” and “oxygen-poor”.
Explain that blood itself is red.
Name an artery by direction.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Labels remain useful in monochrome printing. Avoid colour alone as the indicator.

slides.title: Test another map
body: Trace one complete journey.
Identify one strong label.
Suggest one specific correction.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Teacher offers anonymous or private review. Accept a pupil choosing teacher review over peer exchange.

slides.title: Choose a model improvement
body: Should the next version add capillaries or chambers?
Explain what that extra detail would help show.
slides.notes: Lundy: collect choices, pick one detail to draw next on the board and explain which pupil reasoning influenced it. Capillaries clarify exchange; chambers clarify receiving and pumping.

slides.title: A route in three answers
body: E1. After the lungs, where does blood go?
E2. What makes a vessel an artery?
E3. What powers the movement of blood?
slides.notes: E1: left side of the heart. E2: carries blood away from the heart. E3: contracting heart muscle. E4 on the pupil page explains the blue convention. Collect answers before a public explanation.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: the rescue route
pupilPages.intro: The cards describe a simplified circuit. It is a route map, not an anatomical picture.

cards.title: Route A
cards.text: Right heart → lungs. Blood is oxygen-poor on the way to the lungs.

cards.title: Route B
cards.text: Lungs → left heart. Blood has gained oxygen in the lungs.

cards.title: Route C
cards.text: Left heart → body. Blood delivers oxygen to tissues.

cards.title: Route D
cards.text: Body → right heart. Returning blood is oxygen-poor, not oxygen-free.

cards.title: Vessel key
cards.text: Artery = away from heart. Vein = towards heart. Capillaries allow exchange with tissues.

cards.title: Pump and colour key
cards.text: Heart muscle contracts; valves help prevent backflow. Human blood is red. Blue lines in models mean oxygen-poor.

blocks.prompt: W1. Put A–D in cycle order, starting with A. Where does blood gain oxygen?
W2. Repair “lungs straight to body” and “all veins contain blue blood”.
W3. Name the heart-to-lungs vessel type. Explain using direction.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: follow the token
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Words to use: right heart / lungs / left heart / body.

blocks.prompt: S1. Complete the route: BODY → ____ → ____ → ____ → BODY.
S2. Where does blood gain oxygen?
S3. A vessel carries blood away from the heart. It is an …
S4. Complete: Heart ____ contract to pump ____ . Valves help prevent ____ flow. Word bank: backward / muscles / blood.
S5. Explain what blue means on a blood-flow diagram. What colour is blood?
S6. Draw the complete route with four arrows.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: repair the map
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Labels must remain clear if printed without colour.

blocks.prompt: N1. Draw a complete cycle using both heart sides, lungs and body. Mark where oxygen enters the blood.
N2. Complete the table and explain the rule you used.
N3. Explain the different jobs of heart muscle and valves.
N4. Repair: “The blue vessel must contain blue blood.”

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: audit a teaching model
pupilPages.intro: A good model must be accurate about the relationships it shows.

blocks.prompt: T1. Repair and redraw: right heart → body → lungs → left heart → right heart.
T2. Explain why an oxygen-poor artery is possible. Give the route.
T3. Describe how the heart muscle and valves work together. Which supplies the pumping force?
T4. Identify two limits of a four-box route model. Explain one useful detail to add.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Use direction words, not just colours.

blocks.prompt: E1. Where does blood travel immediately after the lungs in our route?
E2. What defines an artery?
E3. What produces the force that pumps blood?
E4. What does blue mean in this model? Is blood blue?
Reflection. Which route error can you now explain?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1/R2 blood. R3 oxygen, nutrients or water are acceptable. Oxygen enters blood in the lungs.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 A→B→C→D→A; oxygen enters in lungs. W2 lungs→left heart→body; blood is red, and veins are defined by flow towards the heart. W3 pulmonary artery, because flow is away from the heart; oxygen-poor blue is a diagram convention.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A incorrect: left heart must come before body. B correct. C incorrect: right heart receives blood from body and sends it to lungs.

answers.label: S1–S6
answers.answer: S1 right heart→lungs→left heart. S2 lungs. S3 artery. S4 muscles/blood/backward. S5 blue means oxygen-poor; human blood is red. S6 complete directed loop: right heart→lungs→left heart→body→right heart. Accept any spatial arrangement with correct arrows.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1 correct loop; oxygen gain at lungs. N2 artery/vein/artery/vein; away versus towards heart. N3 muscle contractions pump blood; valves resist backward flow. N4 blue labels oxygen-poor blood on this diagram; it is not actual blue blood.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 right heart→lungs→left heart→body→right heart. T2 pulmonary artery goes away from right heart towards lungs and carries oxygen-poor blood. T3 muscle contraction supplies force; valves help make flow one-way. T4 limits include missing four chambers, capillary exchange detail, vessel branching, actual shapes and relative sizes. A justified useful addition such as capillaries showing oxygen exchange is sufficient.

answers.label: E1–E4 / reflection
answers.answer: E1 left side of heart. E2 carries blood away from heart. E3 contracting heart muscle. E4 oxygen-poor; blood is red. Reflection needs no particular personal response.

answers.label: Assessment and re-teach
answers.answer: Secure: complete route with both heart sides, direction-based vessel definition and pumping-muscle explanation. Re-teach skipped-heart errors with one token traced twice through labelled heart sides. Re-teach blue-blood or all-arteries-oxygen-rich errors by comparing the pulmonary artery with the colour key.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.
No pupil pulse readings or exercise comparison is part of this lesson. Right and left are the person’s anatomical sides, not necessarily the left and right of a page.
For stretch, name atria as receiving chambers and ventricles as pumping chambers if already familiar. Do not let optional chamber names replace accurate core route reasoning.
Blood always remains red in this modelled human system. Oxygen-poor is a relative label, not an assertion of zero oxygen.

Interactive We do uses predict, test and explain; paper cards W1–W3 provide the same decisions. A desk token can trace the model without an animated screen. Movement is optional and pupils control the pace.

interactive.title: Route rescue: predict each destination
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.
